Slides (black — the 2026 deck), the doctor's notes (green), every gift (red) and the Aldughaither summary of the anorectum (grey, at the end).

  • Objectives: anatomy of the anal canal and pelvic floor · focused history and systematic examination (DRE, anoscopy) · recognise and classify benign anorectal conditions · management ladder for each · red flags that mandate urgent referral or biopsy · distinguish anorectal disease from malignancy and IBD.

Surgical anatomy

  • Five landmarks — memorise these and the rest is pattern recognition:
LandmarkKey point
Anal canal3–4 cm, anorectal ring → anal verge
Dentate lineDivides hindgut (columnar, insensate) from proctoderm (squamous, somatic) — decides pain, staging, lymphatics
Internal sphincterInvoluntary smooth muscle (continuation of rectal circular muscle); resting tone ~70–85%
External sphincterVoluntary striated (deep, superficial, subcutaneous), continuous with puborectalis; squeeze pressure
Anorectal ringPalpable ring (puborectalis + upper sphincters) — division causes incontinence
  • Canal ~4 cm in men (~1 cm shorter in women); max dilatation ~2 cm; rectal capacity ~500 mL. Perianal spaces: intersphincteric (tight — abscess very painful; commonest fistula plane), ischioanal (large — pathology may be invisible; always palpate), supralevator (deep — systemic symptoms). The anterior sphincter is shorter in women → more incontinence after surgery.
  • Continence = internal sphincter + external sphincter (pudendal nerve) + puborectalis/levator (anorectal angle) + rectal reservoir. Colitis, proctitis, radiation → urgency through the reservoir, with normal sphincters.
Above the dentate lineBelow the dentate line
EpitheliumColumnarSquamous
ArterySuperior rectal (IMA)Inferior rectal (internal pudendal)
VeinsSuperior rectal → portalInferior rectal → systemic (caval)
LymphaticsInferior mesenteric / internal iliacSuperficial inguinal
SensationVisceral — stretch onlySomatic — richly pain-sensitive
ClinicalInternal haemorrhoids painlessFissures, thrombosed external piles painful
Painless bleeding → think above the line. Painful bleeding → think below the line.

History, red flags & examination

  • Characterise: bleeding (colour, timing — on paper / dripping / mixed, relation to defecation); pain (constant vs defecation-related, sitting, nocturnal pain → sepsis); lump, discharge, itching, soiling.
Red flags: bowel-habit change, weight loss, tenesmus, family history → colonoscopy. Age > 50, anaemia, palpable mass → always exclude cancer before labelling "haemorrhoids". Anaemia + age > 45 + bleeding of any kind → colonoscopy.
  • Doctor's thresholds: > 50 with new symptoms → scope even if a fissure is visible; > 45 + anaemia → colonoscopy; > 45 + bleeding/constitutional symptoms → evaluate rectum and colon.
SymptomPoints to
Bright red on paper / drippingLow anorectal source — haemorrhoids, fissure
Dark/maroon or mixed with stoolProximal — colonoscopy
Sharp, tearing pain with defecationFissure
Constant, severe, throbbing painThrombosed haemorrhoid or abscess — examine before you reassure
Reducible lumpProlapsing internal haemorrhoids
Circumferential full-thickness "rosette"Rectal prolapse
Painful fixed massAbscess first, neoplasm second
  • Painful rectal bleeding, worst during and after defecation → anal fissure. 430 ×4
  • 20-year-old with 3rd-degree haemorrhoids, family history of colon cancer and iron-deficiency anaemia → colonoscopy. 439 ×12
  • Examination: left lateral (Sims) or lithotomy, light, chaperone; inspect (fissures, openings, tags, prolapse — ask to strain) · DRE (tone, masses, tenderness, prostate; clock positions) · anoscopy/proctoscopy (DRE alone misses most internal haemorrhoids) · sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy for red flags or age > 45–50.
  • If pain prevents examination → analgesia/local treatment and re-examine later — never force it.

Haemorrhoids

  • Downward displacement and engorgement of the normal anal vascular cushions (AV anastomoses) — contribute ~15–20% of resting pressure and help sense gas/liquid/solid.
  • Primary cushions at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock (lithotomy): left lateral, right posterior, right anterior.
  • The right posterior (7 o'clock) cushion most often becomes the largest. "Family history" usually reflects shared habits, not genes.
  • Risk factors: habitual — straining, constipation, low-fibre diet, prolonged sitting, pregnancy, obesity, ageing; pathological — chronic diarrhoea (IBD), colon malignancy, portal hypertension, spinal injury, rectal surgery, anal intercourse.
  • Pathogenesis: dilated AV cushions · stretched suspensory fibromuscular stroma · prolapsed rectal mucosa. Internal above, external below the dentate line.
  • Clinical: painless bright-red bleeding with defecation · prolapse · mucoid discharge & pruritus · pain only if complicated (strangulation, thrombosis, abscess).
  • Differentials: fissure, rectal prolapse, abscess, colorectal malignancy (age > 45–50 or red flags).
  • Bleeding + significant pain is not a simple haemorrhoid — think fissure, thrombosis, strangulation, IBD, malignancy.
Goligher gradeProlapseManagement (slide)
IBleeds, no prolapseFibre, fluids, topical agents
IIProlapses on straining, reduces spontaneouslyRubber band ligation
IIIProlapses, needs manual reductionRBL / surgical referral
IVPermanently prolapsed, irreducibleHaemorrhoidectomy

Internal haemorrhoids grades 1st–4th

  • Grades apply only to internal haemorrhoids — external ones have no grade. Notes: grade I–II conservative ± banding/laser; III banding or surgery; IV usually operative.
  • Haemorrhoids that can be manually reduced → grade 3. 438
  • Painless bright red bleeding with prolapse that reduces spontaneously (grade II), no red flags → keyed fibre, stool softeners and topical analgesia (conservative is first-line for every grade; banding next). 442

Complications

  • Thrombosis — sudden severe pain from a clotted external pile → excise within 48–72 h if early. Strangulation — grade IV with compromised supply. Ulceration & bleeding → iron-deficiency anaemia. Infection/abscess (rare).

Management ladder

  • 1. Conservative (basis for every grade): high fibre, fluids, stool softeners, topical agents. 2. Office: rubber band ligation (I–III), sclerotherapy, infrared coagulation. 3. Operative: excisional haemorrhoidectomy or stapled haemorrhoidopexy for III–IV. 4. Emergency: thrombosed external pile — excise within 72 h; otherwise analgesia and sitz baths.
  • Topical nitrates/CCBs are for fissures, not haemorrhoids.
TechniqueKey point
Band ligationOutpatient, grade II–III; avoid on anticoagulants
Open haemorrhoidectomy (Milligan–Morgan) / closed (Ferguson)Most effective for III–IV
Stapled haemorrhoidopexyLess pain, higher long-term recurrence
Laser haemorrhoidoplastyQuicker recovery, costly, less data
Haemorrhoidectomy: preserve anoderm/skin bridges between excisions → prevents anal stenosis; spare the sphincter → prevents incontinence.

Band ligation · closed (Ferguson) haemorrhoidectomy · stapled haemorrhoidopexy · laser

  • Notes: conservative first-line (incl. venoactive drugs, e.g. Daflon); sclerotherapy for patients unfit for surgery; infrared coagulation rarely used. Laser for persistent bleeding grade I–II or small grade III — not grade IV.

Anal fissure

  • A linear ulcer of the lower half of the anal canal, usually posterior midline.
The slide says fissures are more common in men and in the young; the doctor's spoken notes say more common in women (and in the young — stronger sphincter). Both agree it is a disease of younger patients; for "fissure vs fistula" pairs, the notes contrast fissure: female > male with fistula: male > female.

Sphincter anatomy and a posterior midline fissure

  • Pathophysiology: hard stool tears the anoderm → internal sphincter spasm → ↓ anodermal blood flow → ischaemia prevents healing.
  • Classic triad: severe pain on defecation, bright-red bleeding, visible tear.
  • Chronic: oedema (sentinel pile), hypertrophied papilla, visible internal sphincter fibres at the base.
  • Pain has two components: exposed somatic nerve endings + reflex sphincter spasm (lasting ~4 h). Every treatment works by breaking the spasm and restoring perfusion.
AcuteChronic
Duration< 6 weeks> 6 weeks
LookSlit-like tearSentinel pile, hypertrophied papilla, exposed sphincter fibres
TreatmentConservativeChemical sphincterotomy → surgery
  • ~90% in the posterior midline (relative ischaemia). Off-midline or multiple fissures → Crohn's, UC, TB, syphilis, HIV, leukaemia, cancer → biopsy if atypical.
  • Fissure — the false statement → "commonly situated at the lateral side" (lateral fissures suggest specific lesions; chronic fissures form a sentinel pile). 427 ×2
  • Anterior, posterior midline AND lateral fissures → next step colonoscopy (atypical — look for Crohn's). 438 ×3
  • Left lateral fissure with skin tags and a relaxed sphincter → biopsy under anaesthesia (atypical fissure). 438 ×3

Management

  • Medical — first-line, 6–8 weeks: fibre & fluids · sitz baths · topical diltiazem 2% or GTN · botulinum toxin (chemical sphincterotomy, resistant cases).
  • Surgical — failed medical therapy: lateral internal sphincterotomy (LIS) — gold standard, success ~90–95%, small risk of minor incontinence; fissurectomy/flap for selected cases. Avoid sphincterotomy if baseline continence is impaired.
  • LIS divides only part of the internal sphincter, laterally, stopping below the dentate line; main complication faecal incontinence (extra caution in women). Botox lasts ~2–4 months.
  • Persistent severe pain despite topical treatment of a posterior midline fissure, with spasm → lateral internal sphincterotomy. 436

Anorectal abscess

  • Cryptoglandular theory: infected anal gland at the dentate line spreads along four planes.
SiteFrequencyKey point
Perianal60%Most common, at the anal verge
Ischiorectal20%Through the external sphincter into the fossa
Intersphincteric15%Between the sphincters — may be missed; very painful
Supralevator5%Rare — may come from pelvic/abdominal disease; systemic symptoms
  • Antibiotics do NOT treat an abscess — incision & drainage immediately. Cruciate/elliptical incision near the verge; fully deroof the cavity; send pus for culture.
  • Look for a fistula — up to 50% develop fistula-in-ano; counsel and follow up.
  • Antibiotics not routine — for cellulitis, systemic sepsis, diabetes, immunosuppression, valvular disease.
  • Fournier warning: diabetic/immunosuppressed patients deteriorate within hours → broad-spectrum antibiotics + emergency debridement.
  • Notes: ~70% heal after drainage, ~30% develop a fistula; don't hunt for the fistula during acute drainage. A small slit closes in 2–3 days. A high/deep abscess → suspect rectal disease or malignancy.
A perianal abscess that fails to settle after I&D, or keeps recurring, has a fistula until proven otherwise.
  • 6-month-old with an 8-mm tender red perianal swelling → incision and drainage (with antibiotics in an infant). 434 ×2

Anal fistula

  • Abnormal granulation-lined tract between two epithelial surfaces (perianal skin ↔ anal canal/rectum). Low = opens below the anorectal ring; high = at/above it. 26–38% follow an anal abscess. Male:female ~1.8:1, mean age ~38.
  • A fistula won't close because of the granulation lining, foreign body, irradiated tissue, Crohn's, malignancy.
Parks typeCourseFrequency
IntersphinctericIntersphincteric plane → skin~45% — most common
TranssphinctericCrosses both sphincters~30%
SuprasphinctericArches above puborectalis~20%
ExtrasphinctericBypasses the sphincters~5% — look for Crohn's, cancer, trauma
Goodsall's rule: external opening anterior and ≤ 3 cm → straight radial tract; posterior (or anterior > 3 cm) → curves to the posterior midline (6 o'clock).
  • External opening 1.5 cm away in the left posterolateral position → internal opening in the posterior midline 429 ×4; drains externally at the left lateral posterior side → posterior midline. 427 ×2
  • Examine: external opening (distance predicts complexity) · internal opening (hydrogen peroxide bubbles out) · probe gently (false tracts are easy) · MRI pelvis for complex/recurrent/high tracts; endoanal US for sphincter involvement.

External opening, hydrogen-peroxide test and probing

MRI (STIR) and endoanal ultrasound of a fistula tract

  • Diagnostic modality of choice for perianal fistula → MRI. 435
  • Success = complete epithelial healing without residual tract, openings or discharge — "every surgeon's dream".
  • Treatment — eradicate the tract, preserve continence: fistulotomy (low, simple) · seton (loose/draining or cutting) for high/complex · sphincter-sparing: advancement flap, LIFT, fibrin glue/plug · always assess for Crohn's (multiple, recurrent, atypical → MRI + gastroenterology).
Loose (non-cutting) setonCutting seton
Controls sepsis, matures the tractTightened serially to divide the sphincter slowly
Bridge to a later sphincter-sparing repairSuccess 82–100%
Minimal continence riskLong-term incontinence ~12–25%
  • Seton indications: high/complex, recurrent, anterior fistulas in women, Crohn's.
  • Simple low fistula in a young man → fistulotomy. 437 ×2
  • Crohn's with a complex fistula and 4-cm abscess → I&D + seton. 439
  • Recurrent fistula, bloody mucus, tenesmus, unhealthy rectum → keyed Crohn's or UC. 429 ×4

Pilonidal disease

  • In the deep natal cleft (~5 cm above the anus). Acquired: loose hair drawn into midline follicles by friction and suction from sitting → foreign-body reaction ("Jeep disease").
  • Risk: young male, hirsute, deep cleft, obesity, prolonged sitting, poor hygiene.
  • Acute: painful fluctuant abscess with cellulitis. Chronic: midline pits, lateral sinus openings, intermittent discharge.
  • Treatment: I&D the abscess; defer definitive excision until quiescent; off-midline closure (Karydakis, Bascom, rhomboid flap) — lower recurrence than midline closure; hygiene and hair removal after healing.

Midline pits; natal cleft pit and a healed off-midline scar

Functional & structural disorders

Rectal prolapse

  • Partial (mucosal): mucosa + submucosa only. Complete (procidentia): all layers — concentric folds. Internal (intussusception): doesn't protrude.
  • ~6 times more common in women; bimodal — young children and older adults (elderly multiparous women); lax pelvic floor, straining.
Rectal prolapseHaemorrhoids
FoldsCircumferential — concentric ringsRadial grooves
PalpationDouble rectal wallSingle wall
Anal toneDecreased resting and squeezeNormal
  • Clinical: something comes out on straining/coughing/lifting; constipation (58%); mucus; incomplete evacuation; itching.

Rectal prolapse — concentric folds (procidentia) vs mucosal prolapse

  • Abdominal repair (fit patients): ventral mesh rectopexy — lowest recurrence (< 10%), preserves continence and sexual function. Perineal repair (frail): Altemeier (perineal rectosigmoidectomy) or Delorme (mucosal sleeve) — no pelvic dissection, quicker recovery, higher recurrence (~20%). Overall recurrence ~15%.

Faecal incontinence

  • Involuntary loss of stool/flatus — a symptom with an identifiable cause: pudendal neuropathy, idiopathic/ageing, obstetric tear, iatrogenic injury.
  • Ladder: conservative (bulking, loperamide, bowel regimen) → biofeedback → overlapping sphincteroplasty (obstetric/traumatic defect — ~85% initial cure) → sacral nerve stimulation (refractory, intact/repaired sphincter). Treat the cause (prolapse, IBD).

Pruritus ani

  • Chronic perianal itching — idiopathic is the largest group (over-cleaning, moisture, itch–scratch cycle); secondary: haemorrhoids, fissure, fistula, soiling, dermatological, fungal/parasitic, contact dermatitis.
  • Treat the cause; otherwise gentle hygiene, avoid irritants, barrier cream; biopsy atypical, pigmented or non-healing lesions.

Infection, neoplasia & IBD

Anal warts (condyloma acuminata)

  • HPV 6 and 11 (low risk); 16/18 drive dysplasia and anal cancer. Soft cauliflower-like perianal/intra-anal lesions; worse in HIV/immunosuppression; biopsy non-resolving lesions (anal intraepithelial neoplasia).
  • Treatment: podophyllin 15–20% or imiquimod (few, small); cryo/electro/laser (large/resistant); interferons (refractory). Examine the whole canal; screen for other STIs incl. HIV. HPV vaccination prevents most.

Perianal condyloma acuminata

Anal cancer

  • Squamous cell carcinoma near the dentate line; HPV 16/18. High risk: HIV, receptive intercourse, immunosuppression, prior cervical/vulvar dysplasia, smoking. Presents with bleeding, pain, mass, non-healing ulcer.
  • Red flag: 60-year-old with bleeding, weight loss and a palpable inguinal node → anal (or rectal) cancer before haemorrhoids.
  • Work-up: EUA + biopsy · MRI pelvis · CT chest/abdomen/pelvis · inguinal nodes ± biopsy · offer HIV testing.
First-line: Nigro protocol — chemoradiotherapy (5-FU/mitomycin + radiation), organ-preserving and curative for most. APR only for residual/recurrent disease. Follow up with DRE and anoscopy.

Anorectal Crohn's & infective proctitis

  • Crohn's — suspect with multiple, recurrent or off-midline fistulas/fissures, deep cavitating ulcers, oedematous tags, painless complex fistulas → MRI, EUA, colonoscopy, gastroenterology; drain sepsis and use setons — avoid sphincter division in active disease.
  • Infective proctitis/STIs: gonorrhoea, chlamydia (LGV), HSV, syphilis — pain, discharge, tenesmus, bleeding; swabs (NAAT), serology; treat, notify partners, screen for HIV.

Take-home points & practice questions

1. Bleeding > 50 — never label "haemorrhoids" without excluding malignancy. 2. Sepsis — I&D; antibiotics alone aren't treatment. 3. Off-midline fissure/fistula → suspect Crohn's. 4. Sphincter — dividing procedures weigh cure against incontinence. 5. Biopsy any lesion that doesn't resolve. 6. History, DRE and anoscopy resolve most diagnoses without imaging.
Practice Q1 — weightlifter, painless bright-red bleeding, reducible mass at 3 o'clock: which structure is engorged?
AddedInternal haemorrhoidal cushion — above the dentate line (visceral → painless); prolapse = grade II–III. Painful bleeding points below the line (external pile, fissure).
Practice Q2 — chronic posterior fissure with a sentinel pile: best topical agent?
AddedTopical diltiazem 2% — first-line chemical sphincterotomy (~65–70% healing vs ~50% with GTN, fewer headaches). (The slide's tick sits on option a by mistake; the rationale gives diltiazem.)
Practice Q3 — tender fluctuant perianal swelling with cellulitis, stable: first step?
AddedIncision and drainage — antibiotics don't treat an abscess; discuss fistula risk (up to 50%) at follow-up.
Practice Q4 — faecal incontinence 6 weeks after forceps delivery with an anterior external sphincter defect: best targeted therapy?
AddedOverlapping sphincteroplasty (~85% initial cure). Sacral nerve stimulation is for intact-sphincter or refractory cases. (The slide's tick sits on option a by mistake; the rationale gives sphincteroplasty.)
Practice Q5 — 60-year-old, hard irregular mass at the dentate line: strongest risk feature for anal SCC?
AddedHIV-positive with prior perianal warts (HPV 16/18) — never call a hard anal mass "haemorrhoids" before biopsy.

Anorectum

Anorectal Anatomy
1. Overview

The anatomy of the anus and rectum is critical for understanding the evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment of anorectal disorders. The key anatomical structures include the external and internal surfaces, sphincter muscles, vascular supply, lymphatic drainage, and innervation.

2. Surface Anatomy
A. External to Internal Structures
1. Gluteal Skin (Perianal Region)
  • Contains hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands.
  • Common disorders:
    • Anal condyloma (HPV infection)
    • Perianal hidradenitis suppurativa (involves apocrine sweat glands; does not occur in the anal canal).

2. Anoderm (Anal Canal)

  • Begins at the anal verge and ends at the dentate line.
  • Devoid of hair and sweat glands.
  • Highly innervated (somatic nerves) → Pain-sensitive.
  • Common conditions:
    • Anal fissures (often accompanied by a sentinel tag and hypertrophied anal papilla).
    • Anal stenosis (post-hemorrhoidectomy or excessive anoderm excision).

3. Anal Transitional Zone

  • Lies between the anoderm and rectal mucosa.
  • Contains squamous, cuboidal, transitional, and columnar epithelium.
  • Columnae of Morgagni: Vertical ridges in the anal canal.
  • Anal Crypts & Glands:
    • Originate here and extend variably into deeper tissues.
    • Common site of infection → Leads to anal abscesses & fistulas.

4. Rectal Mucosa

  • Begins above the dentate line.
  • Contains engorged vessels responsible for internal hemorrhoids.
  • Viscerally innervated (not pain-sensitive).
3. Vascular Supply
A. Arterial Supply
ArteryOriginSupply
Superior Rectal ArteryInferior mesenteric arteryUpper & middle rectum
Middle Rectal ArteriesInternal iliac arteriesMiddle & lower rectum
Inferior Rectal ArteriesInternal pudendal arteriesAnal canal & sphincters
  • Hemorrhoidal Vessels:
  • Not true veins → Arteriovenous connections with pulsatile flow.
  • Anchored by Treitz muscle.
  • Weakening of these attachments → Hemorrhoidal prolapse.
B. Venous Drainage

Superior RectalInferior mesenteric veinPortal system
Vein

Inferior RectalPudendal veins → Internal iliacSystemic
Veinsveinscirculation
  • Clinical Importance:
  • Communication between portal & systemic venous systems can lead to rectal varices in portal hypertension.
  • Low rectal cancers can spread via both the portal and systemic circulation.
4. Lymphatic Drainage
  • Region Lymphatic Drainage
Above dentate line Inferior mesenteric & internal iliac nodes
Below dentate line Inguinal lymph nodes
Lower rectum
    • Inguinal & inferior mesenteric nodes
  • Clinical Relevance:
  • Anal canal cancers below the dentate line → Metastasize to inguinal nodes.
  • Rectal cancers → Spread to mesenteric & iliac nodes.
5. Nervous System
A. Innervation of the Anorectum
RegionInnervationClinical Importance
Above theAutonomic (sympathetic & parasympathetic)No pain sensation → Allows
dentate linepainless internal hemorrhoid
(Rectum)ligation
Below the dentate line (Anus)Somatic (pudendal nerve)Highly sensitive → Painful external hemorrhoids & fissures
  • Sympathetic fibers (L1-L3):
  • Pass through the inferior mesenteric plexus → Superior hypogastric plexus → Pelvic plexus.
  • Injury can cause bladder & sexual dysfunction.
  • Parasympathetic fibers (S2-S4):
  • Pelvic nerves → Pelvic plexus.
  • Regulates defecation.
6. Anal Sphincter Complex
A. Internal Anal Sphincter (IAS)
  • Involuntary smooth muscle.
  • Maintains anal resting tone.
  • Innervated by autonomic nerves (sympathetic & parasympathetic).
  • Inhibited during defecation.
B. External Anal Sphincter (EAS)
  • Voluntary skeletal muscle.
  • Maintains anal squeeze pressure.
  • Innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4).
  • Coordinates with pelvic floor muscles.
C. Pelvic Floor & Support Structures
  • Puborectalis & Levator Ani Muscles:
  • Creates a sling around the rectum.
  • Maintains the anorectal angle → Key in fecal continence.
7. Clinical Applications
A. Hemorrhoids
  • Internal hemorrhoids:
  • Above the dentate line (painless).
  • Commonly prolapse & bleed.
  • Can be treated with rubber band ligation.
  • External hemorrhoids:
  • Below the dentate line (painful).
  • Requires anesthesia for surgical excision.
B. Anal Fistulas & Abscesses
  • Originate from blocked anal glands in the crypts.
  • Can lead to perianal, intersphincteric, or ischiorectal abscesses.
C. Rectal Prolapse vs. Hemorrhoidal Prolapse
  • Hemorrhoidal prolapse:
  • Radial folds seen on examination.
  • Rectal prolapse:
  • Circumferential folds.
D. Fecal Incontinence
  • Causes:
  • Childbirth trauma (affects EAS).
  • Neurologic diseases (MS, diabetes, scleroderma).
  • Surgical injury (sphincterotomy, fistulotomy).
  • Evaluation:
  • Endoanal ultrasound to assess sphincter integrity.
  • Surgical Management:
  • Sphincter repair for injuries.
  • Sphincter-sparing techniques for complex fistulas.
E. Pudendal Nerve Injury
  • Results in loss of voluntary anal sphincter control.
  • Occurs with pelvic surgery or prolonged vaginal delivery.

B. Diagnostic Approach
  • Acute, painful lump at anus → Likely thrombosed external hemorrhoid.
  • Pain + swelling + fever → Suspect anorectal abscess.
  • Sharp, "knife-like" pain during defecation → Suggests anal fissure.
  • Chronic pain, burning → Consider neuralgia or levator ani syndrome.
  • Exam limitations: Most patients with severe pain cannot tolerate digital rectal exam; consider exam under anesthesia if uncertain.

B. Diagnostic Approach
1. History:
  • Bright red blood on toilet paper → Likely anal fissure or hemorrhoids.
  • Blood mixed with stool → Concern for rectal cancer or colitis.
  • Large-volume bleeding → Consider diverticular disease.

2. Physical Exam & Workup:

  • Inspection & anoscopy: Identify hemorrhoids, fissures, proctitis.
  • Endoscopy required:
    • <40 years old, no family history → Flexible sigmoidoscopy.
    • >40 years old or high-risk → Colonoscopy.

  • Biopsy for any suspicious or non-healing lesion.

B. Diagnostic Approach
1. History & Exam:
  • History of abscess + purulent discharge → Likely anal fistula.
  • Straining + sensation of prolapse → Likely mucosal prolapse.
  • Bloody discharge + systemic symptoms → Consider proctitis or rectal cancer.

2. Workup:

  • Anoscopy for local pathology (fistula, hemorrhoids, prolapse).
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy for suspected IBD, cancer, or unexplained bleeding.
  • If incontinence suspected → Consider anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound.
Hemorrhoids
1. Definition and Pathophysiology
  • Hemorrhoids are vascular structures in the lower rectum and anal canal, composed of arteriovenous connections with pulsatile flow.
  • External hemorrhoids: Located below the dentate line, covered by anoderm or skin.
  • Internal hemorrhoids: Located above the dentate line, covered by mucosa.
Pathogenesis
  • Caused by increased intra-abdominal pressure from:
  • Constipation
  • Straining
  • Diarrhea
  • Pregnancy
  • Prolonged sitting
  • Weakening of Treitz muscle leads to prolapse.
2. Classification of Hemorrhoids
A. Internal Hemorrhoid Grading
GradeDescription
IProminent but no prolapse
IIProlapse but spontaneously reduces
IIIProlapse and requires manual reduction
IVProlapse and irreducible, may be incarcerated/gangrenous
3. Signs and Symptoms
TypeSymptoms
External HemorrhoidsPainful lump, swelling, bleeding (if thrombosed)
Internal HemorrhoidsPainless bleeding, prolapse, pressure-like discomfort
ComplicationsAnemia, Incarceration, Gangrene, Necrosis
4. Diagnosis
  • Thrombosed external hemorrhoids: Purplish swelling at anus.
  • External hemorrhoids with chronic tags: Persistent skin protrusions.
  • Internal hemorrhoids: Diagnosed with anoscopy, often not palpable on digital rectal exam.

  • Hemorrhoids: Radial mucosal folds
  • Rectal prolapse: Circumferential folds

A. Office-Based Procedures
1. Rubber Band Ligation (Preferred)
  • Best for Grades I-III
  • Rubber band placed above dentate line → ischemia → hemorrhoid sloughs in 5-10 days.
  • Complications: Rare sepsis, urinary retention, delayed bleeding.

2. Sclerotherapy

  • Grades I-II
  • Sclerosing agent (phenol in oil) injected → fibrosis & shrinkage.
  • Complications: Necrosis, perforation.

3. Infrared Coagulation

  • Grades I-II
  • Infrared thermal energy applied to hemorrhoids → shrinkage.
  • Complications: Bleeding, necrosis.
B. Surgical Treatment (For Grades III-IV)
1. Excisional Hemorrhoidectomy (Gold Standard)
  • Complete removal of hemorrhoids.
  • Most effective for large, recurrent, Grade III-IV hemorrhoids.
  • Complications:
    • Pain
    • Urinary retention
    • Bleeding
    • Anal stenosis (if excessive tissue removed).

2. Stapled Hemorrhoidopexy

  • Best for circumferential Grade II-III hemorrhoids.
  • Removes redundant mucosa, lifts hemorrhoids.
  • Less pain, but higher recurrence rate.
  • Unique complications: Rectovaginal fistula, rectal obstruction.

3. Doppler-Guided Hemorrhoidectomy

  • Ligation of hemorrhoidal arteries using Doppler guidance.
  • Preserves mucosa, less pain than excisional surgery.
  • Long-term efficacy still under study.
7. Prevention and Prognosis
  • Key preventive measures:
  • High-fiber diet (25-30g daily)
  • Adequate hydration
  • Avoid prolonged sitting/straining
  • Regular exercise
  • Limit time on the toilet
  • Prognosis:
  • Lifestyle modifications reduce recurrence.
  • Office-based procedures (banding, sclerotherapy) effective for Grades I-III.
  • Surgical treatment reserved for severe cases.

1. Definition and Pathophysiology
  • Anal fissure: A tear in the anoderm (lining of the anal canal).
  • Typically found in the posterior (90%) or anterior (10%) midline.

Pilonidal Disease
1. Definition and Etiology
  • Pilonidal disease is a chronic infection that occurs in the gluteal cleft (most commonly in the sacrococcygeal region).
  • The term pilonidal means "nest of hair," reflecting its association with hair entrapment.
  • It primarily affects young men (3:1 male-to-female ratio), with a peak incidence between 16-25 years.
  • Risk Factors:
  • Hairy individuals (hair acts as a foreign body).
  • Prolonged sitting (e.g., office workers, drivers).
  • Poor hygiene or excessive sweating.
  • Obesity (increased moisture and friction).
  • Family history (possible genetic predisposition).
2. Pathophysiology
  • The deep gluteal cleft creates a vacuum effect, leading to the suction of loose hairs into the skin pits.
  • The hair and debris in these pits act as foreign bodies, causing chronic inflammation, abscess formation, and sinus tracts.
  • Pilonidal disease can manifest as acute abscesses, chronic draining sinuses, or recurrent non-healing wounds.

A. Non-Surgical Management
1. Conservative Management (for mild cases)
  • Shaving the gluteal cleft (reduces hair accumulation).
  • Daily hygiene: Encourage showering and keeping the area dry.
  • Warm soaks: Help relieve mild symptoms.
  • Weight loss: Reduces risk of recurrence.
  • Avoid prolonged sitting.

  • Preferred incision site: Lateral (off-midline) to prevent poor healing.
  • No packing is required, but daily hygiene is essential.
  • Antibiotics: Only needed in immunocompromised patients, cellulitis, or sepsis.

Tumors of the Anal Canal
1. Anal Cancer
Clinical Findings
  • Rare (~2% of all colorectal malignancies).
  • Histologic subtypes:
  • Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) – most common.
  • Basaloid, mucoepidermoid, epidermoid, and cloacogenic cancers.
  • Risk Factors:
  • HPV infection (HPV-16, HPV-18).
  • HIV, immunosuppression.
  • Anoreceptive intercourse.
  • Tobacco use.
Symptoms
  • Variable presentation (often initially misdiagnosed as benign anorectal disease).
  • Slow-growing tumors.
  • Common symptoms:
  • Pain, bleeding, mass sensation, pruritus, tenesmus, incontinence (advanced cases).
  • Physical Exam:
  • Digital rectal exam (DRE) and anoscopy:
    • Assess tumor size, location, fixation, consistency.
  • Inguinal adenopathy:
    • Palpable nodes should be biopsied (FNA or core biopsy).
  • Imaging & Staging:
  • Endoanal ultrasound & MRI → Primary tumor assessment.
  • CT/PET scan → Distant metastases & nodal involvement.

Treatment Standard Therapy: Chemoradiation (Nigro Protocol)

  • 5-FU + Mitomycin C + Radiation.
  • High response rate (85%-90%).
  • Sphincter preservation.
  • Lower recurrence compared to surgery.
Alternative Approaches
  • Radiation alone (for frail patients).
  • Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT) (reduces toxicity).
  • Salvage Surgery (APR - Abdominoperineal Resection)
  • Reserved for persistent or recurrent disease after chemoradiation.
  • 5-year survival post-APR: 24%-58%.
  • Common complication: Poor wound healing.
Management of Lymph Node Disease
  • Inguinal node involvement:
  • Chemoradiation (90% response rate).
  • Groin dissection NOT routinely recommended unless persistent disease.
Response & Surveillance
  • Response assessed ~8 weeks post-chemoradiation.
  • 85%-90% achieve complete response.
  • Partial response → Close monitoring.
  • Persistent/progressive disease → Biopsy & consider salvage APR.
  • Follow-up:
  • DRE, anoscopy, and inguinal node assessment every 3-6 months (first 2 years), then every 6-12 months (up to 5 years).
  • Routine imaging controversial but commonly done.
Prognosis
  • Complete response rates ~90% for smaller tumors.
  • 5-year survival:
  • Small tumors: 70%-90%.
  • Advanced/recurrent disease: 24%-58% (post-APR).
2. Melanoma of the Anal Canal
Overview
  • 3rd most common GI melanoma.
  • 2%-4% of all anorectal tumors.
  • Highly aggressive with poor prognosis.
Clinical Findings
  • Symptoms:
  • Pain, bleeding, mass, tenesmus, weight loss.
  • Inguinal lymphadenopathy (advanced cases).
  • Change in stool caliber (rectal obstruction).
  • Physical Exam:
  • Pigmented, raised lesions.
  • 20%-30% are amelanotic → Can mimic benign disease.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Biopsy with immunohistochemistry (S-100, HMB-45, Melan-A staining).
Treatment
  • Surgery is the only curative option.
  • No proven benefit for chemotherapy or radiation.
  • Two surgical approaches:
  • Wide Local Excision (preferred):
    • For localized disease.
    • Preserves sphincter function.
  • Abdominoperineal Resection (APR):
    • For large, deeply invasive tumors.
    • Does not improve survival.
    • High morbidity.
Prognosis
  • Extremely poor due to late presentation.
  • Survival rates:
  • 6%-28% overall.
  • <10% for metastatic disease.
  • Median survival:
  • 12-18 months.
